desc:
A reverse pair is a pair of indices (i, j) with i < j and nums[i] > 2 * nums[j]. Return the number of reverse pairs in nums.

Do the comparison with exact arithmetic (in languages with 32-bit integers, 2 * nums[j] can overflow, so widen to 64 bits first).

For example, [1, 3, 2, 3, 1] gives 2, from the pairs of values (3, 1) at indices (1, 4) and (3, 1) at indices (3, 4). The array [2, 4, 3, 5, 1] gives 3.
hints: Checking all pairs is O(n<sup>2</sup>), about 12 million checks at the largest size, which is the baseline to beat. Think about divide and conquer on the array.
Split into a left and right half and count the pairs that cross the middle, plus the pairs fully inside each half (recursion). Sorting each half first makes the crossing count easy.

With both halves sorted, walk through the left half in ascending order and move a pointer j forward in the right half while 2 * right[j] < left[i]; the pointer never moves back, and j is the number of valid partners for left[i].
editorial: This is the merge-sort inversion count with a twist: the counting condition (nums[i] > 2 * nums[j]) is not the same as the sort order. So we count first and merge afterwards. For each half we get its sorted version and its internal pair count by recursion. To count the crossing pairs, iterate over the sorted left half; as left[i] grows, the set of right elements with 2 * right[j] < left[i] only grows, so a single moving pointer over the sorted right half gives all counts in linear time. Then merge the two halves and return.

Each level of the recursion does linear work and there are log n levels, so the total is O(n log n). A Fenwick tree over the compressed values of all nums[i] and 2 * nums[i] achieves the same bound. Negative numbers need no special handling since the whole argument only uses the ordering of the numbers.
